Minimum Rates of Approximate Sufficient Statistics

Masahito Hayashi    † Fellow, IEEE    Vincent Y. F. Tan    ‡ Senior Member, IEEE ††thanks: †Masahito˜Hayashi is with the Graduate School of Mathematics, Nagoya University, and the Center for Quantum Technologies (CQT), National University of Singapore (Email: masahito@math.nagoya-u.ac.jp). ††thanks: $‡$Vincent˜Y.˜F. Tan is with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore (Email: vtan@nus.edu.sg).††thanks: This paper was presented in part˜[1] at the 2017 International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT) in Aachen, Germany.††thanks: MH is partially supported by a MEXT Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (B) No.˜16KT0017. The Centre for Quantum Technologies is funded by the Singapore Ministry of Education and the National Research Foundation as part of the Research Centres of Excellence programme.††thanks: VYFT is partially supported an NUS Young Investigator Award (R-263-000-B37-133) and a Singapore Ministry of Education Tier 2 grant “Network Communication with Synchronization Errors: Fundamental Limits and Codes” (R-263-000-B61-112).
Abstract

Given a sufficient statistic for a parametric family of distributions, one can estimate the parameter without access to the data. However, the memory or code size for storing the sufficient statistic may nonetheless still be prohibitive. Indeed, for nn independent samples drawn from a kk-nomial distribution with d=k−1d=k-1 degrees of freedom, the length of the code scales as d​log⁡n+O⁡(1)d\log n+O(1). In many applications, we may not have a useful notion of sufficient statistics (e.g., when the parametric family is not an exponential family) and we also may not need to reconstruct the generating distribution exactly. By adopting a Shannon-theoretic approach in which we allow a small error in estimating the generating distribution, we construct various approximate sufficient statistics and show that the code length can be reduced to d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1). We consider errors measured according to the relative entropy and variational distance criteria. For the code constructions, we leverage Rissanen’s minimum description length principle, which yields a non-vanishing error measured according to the relative entropy. For the converse parts, we use Clarke and Barron’s formula for the relative entropy of a parametrized distribution and the corresponding mixture distribution. However, this method only yields a weak converse for the variational distance. We develop new techniques to achieve vanishing errors and we also prove strong converses. The latter means that even if the code is allowed to have a non-vanishing error, its length must still be at least d2​log⁡n\frac{d}{2}\log n.

Index Terms: 
Approximate sufficient statistics, Minimum rates, Memory size reduction, Minimum description length, Exponential families, Pythagorean theorem, Strong converse

I Introduction

The notion of sufficient statistics is a fundamental and ubiquitous concept in statistics and information theory [2, 3]. Consider a random variable X∈𝒳X\in\mathcal{X} whose distribution PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z} depends on an unknown parameter z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}. Typically in detection and estimation problems, we are interested in learning the unknown parameter zz. In this case, it is often unnecessary to use the full dataset XX. Rather a function of the data Y=f⁡(X)∈𝒴Y=f(X)\in\mathcal{Y} usually suffices. If there is no loss in the performance of learning ZZ given YY relative to the case when one is given XX, then YY is called a sufficient statistic relative to the family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}. We may then write

PX|Z=z​(x)=∑y∈𝒴PX|Y​(x|y)​PY|Z=z​(y),∀(x,z)∈𝒳×𝒵P_{X|Z=z}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}P_{X|Y}(x|y)P_{Y|Z=z}(y),\;\forall\,(x,z)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Z} (1)

or more simply that X⊸--Y⊸--ZX\mathrel{\multimap}\joinrel\mathrel{-}\joinrel\mathrel{\mkern-6.0mu}\joinrel\mathrel{-}Y\mathrel{\multimap}\joinrel\mathrel{-}\joinrel\mathrel{\mkern-6.0mu}\joinrel\mathrel{-}Z forms a Markov chain in this order. Because YY is a function of XX, it is also true that I⁡(Z,X)=I⁡(Z,Y)I(Z;X)=I(Z;Y). This intuitively means that the sufficient statistic YY provides as much information about the parameter ZZ as the original data XX does.

For concreteness in our discussions, we often (but not always) regard the family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} as an exponential family [4], i.e., PX|Z=z∝exp⁡(∑izi​Yi​(x))P_{X|Z=z}\propto\exp\big(\sum_{i}z_{i}Y_{i}(x)\big). This class of distributions is parametrized by a set of natural parameters z={zi}z=\{z_{i}\} and a set of natural statistics Y​(x)={Yi​(x)}Y(x)=\{Y_{i}(x)\}, which is a function of the data. The natural statistics or maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) are known to be sufficient statistics of the exponential family. In many applications, large datasets are prevalent. The one-shot model described above will then be replaced by an nn-shot one in which the dataset consists of nn independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables Xn=(X1,X2,…,Xn)X^{n}=(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}) each distributed according to PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z} where the exact zz is unknown. If the support of XX is finite, the distribution is a kk-nomial distribution (a discrete distribution taking on at most kk values) and the empirical distribution or type [5] of XnX^{n} is a sufficient statistic for learning zz. However, the number of types with denominator nn on an alphabet with kk values is (n+k−1k−1)=Θ⁡(nk−1)\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}=\Theta(n^{k-1}) [5]. We are interested in this paper in the “memory size” to store the various types. We imagine that each type is allocated a single storage location in the memory stack and the memory size is the number of storage locations. Thus, the memory size required to estimate parameter zz in a maximum likelihood manner (or distribution PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z}) is at least Θ⁡(nk−1)\Theta(n^{k-1}) if the (index of the) type is stored. The exponent d=k−1d=k-1 here is the number of degrees of freedom in the distribution family, i.e., the dimensionality of the space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} that zz belongs to. Can we do better than a memory size of Θ⁡(nd)\Theta(n^{d})? The answer to this question depends on the strictness of the recoverability condition of PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z}. If PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z} is to be recovered exactly, then the Markov condition in (1) is necessary and no reduction of the memory size is possible. However, if PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z} is to be recovered only approximately, we can indeed reduce the memory size. This is one motivation of the current work.

In addition, going beyond exponential families, for general distribution families, we do not necessarily have a useful and universal notion of sufficient statistics. Thus, we often focus on local asymptotic sufficient statistics by relaxing the condition for sufficient statistics. For example, under suitable regularity conditions [6, 7, 8], the MLE forms a set of local asymptotic sufficient statistics. However, there is no prior work that discusses the required memory size if we allow the sufficient statistics to be approximate in some appropriate sense. To address this issue, we introduce the notion of the minimum coding length of certain asymptotic sufficient statistics and show that it is d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1), where dd is the dimension of the parameter of the family of distribution. Hence, the minimum coding rate is the pre-log coefficient d2\frac{d}{2}, improving over the original dd when exact sufficient statistics are used. Here, we also notice that the locality condition can be dropped. That is, our asymptotic sufficient statistics works globally. This is another motivation for the current paper.

I-A Related Work

Our problem is different from lossy and lossless conventional source coding [9, 10] because we do not seek to reconstruct the data XnX^{n} but rather a distribution on 𝒳n\mathcal{X}^{n}. Hence, we need to generalize standard data compression schemes. Such a generalization has been discussed in the context of quantum data compression by Schumacher [11]. Here, the source that generates the state cannot be directly observed. Schumacher’s encoding process involves compressing the original dataset into a memory stack with a smaller size. The decoding process involves recovering certain statistics of the data to within a prescribed error bound δ≥0\delta\geq 0.

Reconstruction of distributions has also been studied in the context of the information bottleneck (IB) method [12, 13, 14]. In the IB method, given a joint distribution PX,YP_{X,Y}, one seeks to find the best tradeoff between accuracy and complexity when summarizing a random variable XX and an observed and correlated variable YY. More precisely, one finds a conditional distribution PX~|XP_{\tilde{X}|X} that minimizes I⁡(X~,X)−β​I​(X~,Y)I(\tilde{X};X)-\beta I(\tilde{X};Y) where β>0\beta>0 can be regarded as a Lagrange multiplier. The random variable X~\tilde{X} is then regarded as a summarized version of XX. Although such a formalism is a generalization of the notion of sufficient statistics from parametric statistics to arbitrary distributions, it differs from the present work because our work is concerned with finding minimum rates in an asymptotic and information-theoretic framework.

Recently, Yang, Chiribella and Hayashi [15] extended Schumacher’s [11] compression system to a special quantum model. In particular, the authors considered a notion of approximate sufficient statistics in the quantum setting [16, 17] when the data is generated in an i.i.d. manner. They considered only the so-called blind setting [18, Ch. 10] and also only showed a weak converse. We note that there have been recent developments of the notion of approximate sufficient statistics and approximate Markov chains in the quantum information literature [19, 20] but the problem studied here and the objectives are different from the existing works.

Another related line of works in the classical information theory literature are the seminal ones by Rissanen on universal variable-length source coding and model selection [21, 22]. Under the minimum description length (MDL) framework, he introduced a two-step encoding process to obtain a prefix-free source code for nn data samples generated from a mixture of i.i.d. distributions. The purpose of Rissanen’s compression system is to obtain a compression system for data generated under a mixture distribution. He showed that when the dimensionality of the data is dd, the optimal redundancy over the Shannon entropy is d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1). Merhav and Feder [23] extended Rissanen’s analysis to both the minimax and Bayesian (maximin) senses. Clarke and Barron [24, 25] refined Rissanen’s analysis and determined the constant (in asymptotic expansions) under various regularity assumptions. While we make heavy use of some of Rissanen’s coding ideas and Clarke and Barron’s asymptotic expansions for the relative entropy between a parametrized distribution and a mixture, the problem setting we study is different. Indeed, the main ideas in Rissanen’s work [21, 22] are only helpful for us to establish the achievability parts of our theorems with non-zero asymptotic error for the relative entropy criterion (see Lemma 1). Similarly, the main results of Clarke and Barron’s work [24, 25] can only lead to a weak converse under the variational distance criterion (see Lemma 4). Hence, we need to develop new coding techniques and converse ideas to satisfy the more stringent constraints on the code sequences.

I-B Main Contributions and Techniques

We provide a precise Shannon-theoretic problem formulation for compression for the model parameter zz with an allowable asymptotic error δ≥0\delta\geq 0 on the reconstructed distribution. This error is measured under the relative entropy and variational distance criteria. We use some of Rissanen’s ideas for encoding in [21, 22] to show that the memory size can be reduced to approximately Θ⁡(nd2)\Theta(n^{\frac{d}{2}}) resulting in a coding length of d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1). Note that Rissanen [21, 22] did not explicitly provide the decoders for the problem he considered; we explicitly specify various decoders. Moreover, assuming that the parametric family of distributions is an exponential family [4], we also improve on the evaluations that are inspired by Rissanen (see Lemma 2). In particular, for exponential families, we propose codes whose asymptotic errors measured according to the relative entropy criterion are equal to zero. Furthermore, we consider two separate settings known as the blind and visible settings. In the former, the encoder can directly observe the dataset XnX^{n}; in the latter the encoder directly observes the parameter of interest zz. The differences between these two settings are discussed in more detail in [18, Ch. 10]. The visible setting may appear to be less natural but such a generalized setting is useful for the proofs of the converse parts. Yang, Chiribella and Hayashi [15] only considered the special case of the qubit model. They also only considered the blind setting. We consider both blind and visible settings and show, somewhat surprisingly, that the coding length is essentially unchanged.

Another significant contribution of our work is in the strengthening of the converse in [15]. In our strong converse proof for the relative entropy error criterion, we employ the Pythagorean theorem for relative entropy, a fundamental concept in information geometry [26]. Furthermore, we use Clarke and Barron’s formula [24, 25] to provide a weak converse under the variational distance error criterion. This clarifies the relation between our problem and Clarke and Barron’s formula [24, 25]. We significantly strengthen this method to obtain a strong converse (see Lemma 6); in contrast [15] only proves a weak converse. That is, we show that if the error is allowed to be non-vanishing (even if it is arbitrarily large for the relative entropy criterion and arbitrarily close to 22 for the variational distance criterion), we would still require a memory size of at least nd⁡(12−η)n^{d(\frac{1}{2}-\eta)} for any η>0\eta>0 for all sufficiently large nn.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we formulate the problem precisely. We state the main result Theorem 1 in Section III. The results are discussed in the context of exact sufficient statistics and exponential families in Section IV. We prove the direct parts of Theorem 1 in Section V, leveraging ideas from Rissanen’s seminal works [21, 22] on universal data compression. We prove the converse parts of Theorem 1 in Section VI by leveraging the Pythagorean theorem in information geometry [26] and Clarke and Barron’s formula [24, 25]. We conclude our discussion in Section VII.

II Problem Formulation

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a set and let 𝒫⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) denote the set of distributions (e.g., probability mass functions) on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We consider a family of distributions {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵⊂𝒫⁡(𝒳)\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) parametrized by a vector parameter z∈𝒵⊂ℝdz\in\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}. We assume that nn independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables Xn=(X1,…,Xn)X^{n}=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}) each taking values in 𝒳\mathcal{X} and drawn from PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z}. The underlying parameter ZZ, which is random, follows a distribution μ⁡(d​z)\mu(\mathrm{d}z), which is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. We will often use the following notations: Given conditional distributions PX|YP_{X|Y} and PY|ZP_{Y|Z}, respectively let the joint and marginal probabilities conditioned on Z=zZ=z be

(PX|Y×PY|Z)​(x,y|z)\displaystyle(P_{X|Y}\times P_{Y|Z})(x,y|z) :=PX|Y​(x|y)​PY|Z​(y|z),and\displaystyle:=P_{X|Y}(x|y)P_{Y|Z}(y|z),\quad\mbox{and} (2)
(PX|Y⋅PY|Z)​(x|z)\displaystyle(P_{X|Y}\cdot P_{Y|Z})(x|z) :=∑y(PX|Y×PY|Z)​(x,y|z).\displaystyle:=\sum_{y}(P_{X|Y}\times P_{Y|Z})(x,y|z). (3)

Standard asymptotic notation such as o⁡(⋅)o(\cdot), O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot), Ω⁡(⋅)\Omega(\cdot) and Θ\Theta will be used throughout; fn=o⁡(gn)f_{n}=o(g_{n}) iff lim¯n→∞⁡|fn/gn|=0\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}|f_{n}/g_{n}|=0, fn=O⁡(gn)f_{n}=O(g_{n}) iff lim¯n→∞⁡|fn/gn|<∞\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}|f_{n}/g_{n}|<\infty, fn=Ω⁡(gn)f_{n}=\Omega(g_{n}) iff gn=O⁡(fn)g_{n}=O(f_{n}) and fn=Θ⁡(gn)f_{n}=\Theta(g_{n}) iff fn=O⁡(gn)f_{n}=O(g_{n}) and fn=Ω⁡(gnCLOSEf_{n}=\Omega(g_{n}). II-A Definitions of Codes

We consider two classes of codes [18, Ch. 10] for the problem of interest:

Definition 1 (Blind code).

A size MnM_{n} blind code of 𝒞b,n:=(fb,n,φn)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}:=(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n}) consists of

  • •

    A stochastic encoder (transition kernel) fb,n:𝒳n→𝒴n:={1,…,Mn}f_{\mathrm{b},n}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\mathcal{Y}_{n}:=\{1,\ldots,M_{n}\};

  • •

    A decoder φn:𝒴n→𝒫⁡(𝒳n)\varphi_{n}:\mathcal{Y}_{n}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}^{n}).

Observe that this definition of a code is similar to that for source coding except that the decoder outputs distributions on 𝒳n\mathcal{X}^{n} instead of length-nn strings in 𝒳n\mathcal{X}^{n}. We often consider a more relaxed condition for the encoder as follows. In the visible setting, the encoder does not only have access to the random vector XnX^{n} but also to the parameter z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}.

Definition 2 (Visible code).

A size MnM_{n} visible code 𝒞v,n:=(fv,n,φn)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}:=(f_{\mathrm{v},n},\varphi_{n}) consists of

  • •

    A stochastic encoder (transition kernel) fv,n:𝒵→𝒴n:={1,…,Mn}f_{\mathrm{v},n}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathcal{Y}_{n}:=\{1,\ldots,M_{n}\};

  • •

    A decoder φn:𝒴n→𝒫⁡(𝒳n)\varphi_{n}:\mathcal{Y}_{n}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}^{n}).

We note that any blind encoder fb,nf_{\mathrm{b},n} can be regarded as a special case of a visible encoder fv,nf_{\mathrm{v},n} because the visible encoder fv,nf_{\mathrm{v},n} can be written in terms of the blind encoder fb,nf_{\mathrm{b},n} and the distribution PX|Z=znP_{X|Z=z}^{n} as follows

fv,n​(z):=∑xn∈𝒳nfb,n​(xn)​PX|Z=zn​(xn),∀z∈𝒵.f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z):=\sum_{x^{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n}}f_{\mathrm{b},n}(x^{n})P_{X|Z=z}^{n}(x^{n}),\quad\forall\,z\in\mathcal{Z}. (4)

II-B Error Criteria

The performance of any code is characterized by two quantities. First, we desire the coding length log⁡Mn=log⁡|𝒴n|\log M_{n}=\log|\mathcal{Y}_{n}| to be as short as possible. Next we desire a small error. To define an error criterion precisely, we notice that the reconstructed distribution on 𝒳n\mathcal{X}^{n} (in the visible case) is φn⋅fv,n​(z)\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z) which is defined as

(φn⋅fv,n(z))(xn)=∑y∈𝒴nPr{fv,n(z)=y}(φn(y))(xn).\displaystyle\!\!\!\big(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)\big)(x^{n})\!=\!\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}\Pr\left\{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)\!=\!y\right\}\big(\varphi_{n}(y)\big)(x^{n}). (5)

Hence the code has a smaller error when the distribution φn⋅fv,n​(z)\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z) is closer to the original distribution PX|Z=znP_{X|Z=z}^{n} for each z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}. To evaluate the difference between the two distributions, we consider an error or fidelity function FF whose inputs are distributions on the same probability space. The average error is defined as

εv​(fv,n,φn):=∫𝒵F⁡(φn⋅fv,n​(z),PX|Z=zn)​μ​(𝑑z).\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}(f_{\mathrm{v},n},\varphi_{n}):=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}F(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z),P_{X|Z=z}^{n})\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z). (6)

For a blind code, in view of (4), we similarly define

εb​(fb,n,φn)=εv​(fb,n⋅PX|Z=zn,φn)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}(f_{\mathrm{b},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n},\varphi_{n})
:=∫𝒵F⁡(φn⋅fv,n⋅PX|Z=zn,PX|Z=zn)​μ​(𝑑z).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad:=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}F(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n},P_{X|Z=z}^{n})\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z). (7)

In this paper, we consider two distance measures, namely the relative entropy D(P∥Q):=∑xP(x)(logP(x)−logQ(x))D(P\|Q):=\sum_{x}P(x)(\log P(x)-\log Q(x)) and the variational distance11 1 Unlike some papers, we define the variational distance without the coefficient of 12\frac{1}{2} multiplying ‖P−Q‖1\|P-Q\|_{1} so 0≤‖P−Q‖1≤20\leq\|P-Q\|_{1}\leq 2. (also known as the total variation distance) ‖P−Q‖1:=∑x|P⁡(x)−Q⁡(x)|\|P-Q\|_{1}:=\sum_{x}|P(x)-Q(x)|. Generalizations of these “distances” to continuous-alphabet distributions are performed in the usual manner. We denote the errors in the blind and visible cases [18, Ch. 10] when we use the variational distance as εb(1)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)} and εv(1)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^{(1)} respectively. Similarly, we denote the errors in the blind and visible cases when we use the relative entropy as εb(2)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)} and εv(2)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^{(2)} respectively. The size of a code 𝒞b,n\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n} is denoted as |𝒞b,n|=|𝒴n||\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}|=|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|.

II-C Definitions of Minimum Compression Rates and Properties

Definition 3 (Minimum Compression Rate).

Let δ≥0\delta\geq 0. We define the minimum compression rate for blind codes for a given parametric family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} as

Rb(i)​(δ):=inf{𝒞b,n}n∈ℕ{lim¯n→∞⁡log⁡|𝒞b,n|log⁡n|lim¯n→∞⁡εb(i)​(𝒞b,n)≤δ}\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(i)}(\delta):=\inf_{\{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}}\left\{\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}|}{\log n}\,\bigg|\,\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(i)}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n})\leq\delta\right\} (8)

where i=1,2i=1,2 denotes whether the error function is the variational distance or relative entropy respectively. In a similar manner, we define the minimum compression rate for visible codes for a given parametric family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} as

Rv(i)​(δ):=inf{𝒞v,n}n∈ℕ{lim¯n→∞⁡log⁡|𝒞v,n|log⁡n|lim¯n→∞⁡εv(i)​(𝒞v,n)≤δ}.\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(i)}(\delta):=\inf_{\{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}}\left\{\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}|}{\log n}\,\bigg|\,\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^{(i)}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n})\leq\delta\right\}. (9)

To understand this definition, we note that if Rb(i)​(δ)=c>0R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(i)}(\delta)=c>0, then for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists a sequence of codes {𝒞b,n}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} with asymptotic error no larger than δ\delta and memory or coding length upper bounded as |𝒞b,n|≤nc+ϵ|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}|\leq n^{c+\epsilon} for nn large enough. Moreover, there is no sequence of codes with with asymptotic error no larger than δ\delta and with |𝒞b,n|≤nc−ϵ|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}|\leq n^{c-\epsilon}.

The definition of the minimum compression rate differs significantly from traditional source coding in Shannon theory [3] where the normalization of the coding length log⁡|𝒞b,n|\log|\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{b},n}| is nn and not log⁡n\log n. Here, we find that the normalization that yields meaningful results is log⁡n\log n as the memory size scales polynomially (and not exponentially) with the blocklength, i.e., |𝒴n|≈nc|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|\approx n^{c} for some c>0c>0.

From the above definitions, it is clear that for any 0≤δ≤δ′0\leq\delta\leq\delta^{\prime} and i=1,2i=1,2, we have

Ra(i)​(δ′)\displaystyle R_{a}^{(i)}(\delta^{\prime}) ≤Ra(i)(δ),a=b,v,\displaystyle\leq R_{a}^{(i)}(\delta),\quad\,\,a=\mathrm{b},\mathrm{v}, (10)
Ra(1)​(0)\displaystyle R_{a}^{(1)}(0) ≤Ra(2)(0),a=b,v,\displaystyle\leq R_{a}^{(2)}(0),\quad\,a=\mathrm{b},\mathrm{v}, (11)
Rv(i)​(δ)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(i)}(\delta) ≤Rb(i)​(δ).\displaystyle\leq R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(i)}(\delta). (12)

Note that (11) follows from Pinsker’s inequality (i.e., D(P∥Q)≥log⁡e2∥P−Q∥12D(P\|Q)\geq\frac{\log\mathrm{e}}{2}\|P-Q\|_{1}^{2}) because a vanishing relative entropy implies the same for the variational distance.

III Assumptions and Main Results

Let JzJ_{z} be the Fisher information matrix of the parametric family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}. This matrix has elements

[Jz]i,j=𝔼z​[(∂log⁡PX|Z=z​(X)∂zi)​(∂log⁡PX|Z=z​(X)∂zj)],[J_{z}]_{i,j}\!=\!\mathbb{E}_{z}\left[\left(\frac{\partial\log P_{X|Z=z}(X)}{\partial z_{i}}\right)\!\left(\frac{\partial\log P_{X|Z=z}(X)}{\partial z_{j}}\right)\right], (13)

where 𝔼z\mathbb{E}_{z} means that we take expectation with respect to X∼PX|Z=zX\sim P_{X|Z=z}. Before we state the main results of this paper, we consider the following assumptions:

  1. (i)

    (Boundedness of Parameter Space) The set 𝒵⊂ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is bounded and has positive Lebesgue measure in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d};

  2. (ii)

    (Euclidean Approximation of Relative Entropy) As z′→zz^{\prime}\to z, the relation

    D(PX|Z=z∥PX|Z=z′)\displaystyle D(P_{X|Z=z}\|P_{X|Z=z^{\prime}})
    =12​∑i,j[Jz]i,j​(zi−zi′)​(zj−zj′)+o⁡(‖z−z′‖2)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}[J_{z}]_{i,j}(z_{i}-z_{i}^{\prime})(z_{j}-z_{j}^{\prime})+o(\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2}) (14)

    holds [27, 28, 26]. We also assume compact convergence (i.e., uniform convergence on compact sets) for (14).

  3. (iii)

    (Asymptotic Efficiency) There exists a sequence of estimators z^n=z^n​(Xn)\hat{z}_{n}=\hat{z}_{n}(X^{n}) for the parameter zz such that

    𝔼z[D(PX|Z=z^n∥PX|Z=z)]=d2​n+o(1n).\mathbb{E}_{z}\left[D(P_{X|Z=\hat{z}_{n}}\|P_{X|Z=z})\right]=\frac{d}{2n}+o\Big(\frac{1}{n}\Big). (15)

    In other words, the estimator z^n\hat{z}_{n} asymptotically achieves the Cramér-Rao lower bound [2, 29] (i.e., 𝔼z​[(z^n−z)​(z^n−z)T]→Jz−1\mathbb{E}_{z}[(\hat{z}_{n}-z)(\hat{z}_{n}-z)^{T}]\to J_{z}^{-1}), so the expectation of (14) with z=znz=z_{n} and z′=zz^{\prime}=z yields (15).

  4. (iv)

    (Local Asymptotic Normality) Fix a point z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} and let z^ML​(Xn)\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}) be the MLE of zz given XnX^{n}. Define the function hz​(Xn)=n​Jz1/2​(z^ML​(Xn)−z)h_{z}(X^{n})=\sqrt{n}J_{z}^{1/2}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})-z) and let ϕ(d)(x):=(2π)−d/2exp(−∥x∥2/2)\phi^{(d)}(x):=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|x\|^{2}/2) be the dd-dimensional standard Gaussian probability density function. The local asymptotic normality condition [7, 6, 8] reads

    ‖ϕ(d)−(PX|Z=z+z′nn⋅hz+z′n−1)‖1→0\Big\|\phi^{(d)}-\Big(P_{X|Z=z+\frac{z^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}}^{n}\cdot h_{z+\frac{z^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}}^{-1}\Big)\Big\|_{1}\to 0 (16)

    for any vector z′∈ℝdz^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

  5. (v)

    (Local Asymptotic Sufficiency) Let ZZ be the random variable corresponding to the parameter zz and let Y′Y^{\prime} be the corresponding MLE z^ML​(Xn)\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}). The local asymptotic sufficiency condition [7, 6, 8] reads

    ‖(PXn|Y′,Z=z⋅PY′|Z=z+z′n)−PX|Z=z+z′nn‖1→0\Big\|\Big(P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Z=z}\cdot P_{Y^{\prime}|Z=z+\frac{z^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}}\Big)-P_{X|Z=z+\frac{z^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}}^{n}\Big\|_{1}\to 0 (17)

    for any vector z′∈ℝdz^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Conditions (i)–(v) are satisfied as long as the parametrized family satisfies some weak smoothness condition [7, 6, 8].

Theorem 1.

Assuming (i), (ii), (iv) and (v), the minimum compression rate for visible codes under the variational distance error criterion

Rv(1)​(δ1)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(1)}(\delta_{1}) =d2,∀δ1∈[0,2).\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2},\quad\forall\,\delta_{1}\in[0,2). (18)

Assuming (i), (ii), the minimum compression rate for visible codes under the relative entropy error criterion

Rv(2)​(δ2)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2}) =d2,∀δ2∈[0,∞).\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2},\quad\forall\,\delta_{2}\in[0,\infty). (19)

Assuming (i), (ii), (iv), and (v), the minimum compression rate for blind codes under the variational distance error criterion

Rb(1)​(δ1′)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(\delta_{1}^{\prime}) =d2,∀δ1′∈[0,2).\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2},\quad\forall\,\delta_{1}^{\prime}\in[0,2). (20)

Assuming (i), (ii), and (iii) the minimum compression rate for blind codes under the relative entropy error criterion

Rb(2)​(δ2′)\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2}^{\prime}) =d2,∀δ2′∈[d2,∞).\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2},\quad\forall\,\delta_{2}^{\prime}\in\Big[\frac{d}{2},\infty\Big). (21)

Furthermore, if (i) holds and {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} is an exponential family [4], (21) can be strengthened to

Rb(2)​(δ2′)=d2,∀δ2′∈[0,∞).\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2}^{\prime})=\frac{d}{2},\quad\forall\,\delta_{2}^{\prime}\in[0,\infty). (22)

The direct and converse parts of this theorem are proved in Sections V and VI respectively. Remarks on and implications of the theorem are detailed in the following section.

IV Connection to Sufficient Statistics and Exponential Families

In this section, we discuss the implications of Theorem 1 in greater detail by relating them to the notion of (exact) sufficient statistics [3, Sec. 2.9]. We first review the fundamentals of sufficient statistics, then motivate the notion of approximate sufficient statistics, provide some background on exponential families, and finally show that if one stores the exact sufficient statistics in the memory 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n}, the memory size would be larger than that prescribed by Theorem 1.

IV-A Review of Sufficient Statistics

Suppose, for the moment, that the blind encoder fb,nf_{\mathrm{b},n} is a deterministic function. When Y=fb,n​(Xn)Y=f_{\mathrm{b},n}(X^{n}) is a sufficient statistic relative to the family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} [3, Sec. 2.9], the conditional distribution PX|Z=z,Y=yn(xn)P_{X|Z=z,Y=y}^{n}(x^{n}) does not depend on zz, i.e., Z⊸--Y⊸--XZ\mathrel{\multimap}\joinrel\mathrel{-}\joinrel\mathrel{\mkern-6.0mu}\joinrel\mathrel{-}Y\mathrel{\multimap}\joinrel\mathrel{-}\joinrel\mathrel{\mkern-6.0mu}\joinrel\mathrel{-}X forms a Markov chain in this order. In this case, we can choose the decoder φn:𝒴n→𝒫⁡(𝒳n)\varphi_{n}:\mathcal{Y}_{n}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}^{n}) as follows

φn(y):=PX|Z=z,Y=yn.\varphi_{n}(y):=P_{X|Z=z,Y=y}^{n}. (23)

Now, noting that PX|Z=zn​({xn:fb,n​(xn)=y})=fb,n⋅PX|Z=zn​(y)P_{X|Z=z}^{n}(\{x^{n}:f_{\mathrm{b},n}(x^{n})=y\})=f_{\mathrm{b},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n}(y) for every yy in the memory 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n}, we have

φn⋅fb,n=∑yfb,n⋅PX|Z=zn​(y)​φn​(y)\displaystyle\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{b},n}=\sum_{y}f_{\mathrm{b},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n}(y)\varphi_{n}(y) (24)
=∑yPX|Z=zn({xn:fb,n(xn)=y})PX|Z=z,Y=yn\displaystyle\quad=\sum_{y}P_{X|Z=z}^{n}(\{x^{n}:f_{\mathrm{b},n}(x^{n})=y\})P_{X|Z=z,Y=y}^{n} (25)
=PX|Z=zn.\displaystyle\quad=P_{X|Z=z}^{n}. (26)

Observe that, in this case, regardless of which error metric we choose, we will attain zero error between the reconstructed distribution φn⋅fb,n\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{b},n} and the original one PX|Z=znP_{X|Z=z}^{n}. However, as we will see, if PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z} is an exponential family the memory size exceeds that prescribed by the various statements in Theorem 1. Thus it is natural to relax the stringent condition in (23) to some approximate versions of it.

IV-C Background on Exponential Families

To put our results in Theorem 1 into context, we regard {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} as an exponential family [4] with parameter space 𝒵⊂ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}. Recall that a parametric family of distributions {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} is called an exponential family if it takes the form

PX|Z=z​(x)=PX​(x)​exp⁡[∑i=1mzi​Yi​(x)−A⁡(z)],P_{X|Z=z}(x)=P_{X}(x)\exp\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_{i}Y_{i}(x)-A(z)\right], (32)

where A⁡(z)A(z), the cumulant generating function of the random vector (Y1​(X),…,Ym​(X))(Y_{1}(X),\ldots,Y_{m}(X)), is defined as

A(z):=log∑xPX(x)exp[∑i=1mziYi(x)].A(z):=\log\sum_{x}P_{X}(x)\exp\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_{i}Y_{i}(x)\right]. (33)

The functions Yi​(x)Y_{i}(x) are known as the sufficient statistics of the exponential family. Another fact that we exploit in the sequel is that for any exponential family, there is an alternative parametrization known as the moment parametrization [4]. There is a one-to-one correspondence between the natural parameter zz and the expectation parameter

ηi​(z):=∂A⁡(z)∂zi=𝔼z​[Yi]=∑xPX|Z=z​(x)​Yi​(x).\eta_{i}(z):=\frac{\partial A(z)}{\partial z_{i}}=\mathbb{E}_{z}[Y_{i}]=\sum_{x}P_{X|Z=z}(x)Y_{i}(x). (34)

Hence, in the following to estimate the natural parameter zz, we can first estimate the moments η⁡(z)=(η1​(z),…,ηm​(z))∈ℋ:={η⁡(z):z∈𝒵}\eta(z)=(\eta_{1}(z),\ldots,\eta_{m}(z))\in\mathcal{H}:=\{\eta(z):z\in\mathcal{Z}\} and then use the one-to-one correspondence to obtain zz.

IV-D An Example: kk-nomial Distributions

Now as a concrete example, we consider a kk-nomial distribution, i.e., the family of discrete distributions that take on k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} values. The set of kk-nomial distributions forms an exponential family with sufficient statistics

Yi(x)={1x=i−1x=i+10else,i=1,…,k−1.\displaystyle Y_{i}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}1&x=i\\ -1&x=i+1\\ 0&\mathrm{else}\end{array}\right.,\quad i=1,\ldots,k-1.

Note that there are other parametrizations. It is known that the vector Y⁡(x):=(Y1​(x),…,Yk−1​(x))Y(x):=(Y_{1}(x),\ldots,Y_{k-1}(x)) allows us to recover information about the unknown parameter zz [26, 30], i.e., Y⁡(x)Y(x) is a sufficient statistic for the kk-nomial distribution.

Given nn i.i.d. data samples from PX|Z=znP_{X|Z=z}^{n}, the exponential family can be written as

PX|Z=zn​(xn)=PXn​(xn)​exp⁡[∑i=1mYi(n)​(xn)​zi−n​A​(z)],P_{X|Z=z}^{n}(x^{n})\!=\!P_{X}^{n}(x^{n})\exp\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}Y_{i}^{(n)}(x^{n})z_{i}\!-\!nA(z)\right]\!,\! (38)

where xn=(x1,…,xn)∈𝒳nx^{n}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathcal{X}^{n} and Yi(n)​(xn):=∑j=1nYi​(xj)Y_{i}^{(n)}(x^{n}):=\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{i}(x_{j}). Thus the vector of sufficient statistics is Y(n)​(xn):=(Y1(n)​(xn),…,Ym(n)​(xn))Y^{(n)}(x^{n}):=(Y_{1}^{(n)}(x^{n}),\ldots,Y_{m}^{(n)}(x^{n})). In the kk-nomial case, the dimension of the exponential family m=k−1m=k-1. It is easy to see that the total number of possibilities of Y(n)​(xn)Y^{(n)}(x^{n}), i.e., the size of the set {Y(n)​(xn):xn∈𝒳n}\{Y^{(n)}(x^{n}):x^{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n}\} is (n+k−1k−1)\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}. This is also the total number of nn-types [5] on an alphabet of size kk. In this case, the required memory size is

log⁡|𝒴n|=log⁡(n+k−1k−1)=(k−1)​log⁡n+O⁡(1).\log|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|=\log\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}=(k-1)\log n+O(1). (39)

Note that k−1=dk-1=d, the dimension of the parameter space 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Thus, the pre-log coefficient is dd, which is twice as large as what the results of Theorem 1 prescribe if we use approximate sufficient statistics in the sense of (31) instead of exact sufficient statistics discussed in Section IV-A. This motivates us to study the fundamental limits of approximate sufficient statistics in the large nn limit to reduce the memory size |𝒴n||\mathcal{Y}_{n}| from nd+o⁡(1)n^{d+o(1)} to nd2+o⁡(1)n^{\frac{d}{2}+o(1)}.

V Proofs of Direct Parts of Theorem 1

In this section, the direct parts (upper bounds) of Theorem 1 will be proved. For logical reasons, the statements in Theorem 1 will not be proved sequentially. Rather we will present the simplest proofs before proceeding to the proofs for more general statements. First, in Section V-A, we will prove semi-direct part for the relative entropy criterion in (21). This immediately leads the proof of the direct part for (19). Next, in Section V-B, we strengthen the direct part for exponential families under the relative entropy criterion in (22). Finally, in Section V-C, we prove the direct part in the blind setting under the variational distance criterion as in (20).

V-A Semi-Direct Part Based On Rissanen’s Minimum Description Length (MDL) Encoder

Here we prove the direct parts for (19) and (21) where the error criterion used is the relative entropy. We present a complete achievability proof in the visible setting, i.e., (19). Notice that (19) implies (18). Under the same error criterion, we show a semi-achievability in the blind setting (i.e., (21)) in which the error does not vanish even in the limit of large nn.

Lemma 1.

Assuming (i), (ii), we have

Rv(2)​(0)≤d2.\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(2)}(0)\leq\frac{d}{2}. (40)

Rb(2)​(d2)≤d2.\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}\Big(\frac{d}{2}\Big)\leq\frac{d}{2}. (41)

Similarly, (41) proves that (21) holds because it implies that Rb(2)​(δ2′)≤d2R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2}^{\prime})\leq\frac{d}{2} for all δ2′∈[d2,∞)\delta_{2}^{\prime}\in[\frac{d}{2},\infty). We also note that (41), which follows from Rissanen’s ideas [21, 22], is rather weak because the asymptotic error is bounded above by d2\frac{d}{2} instead of 00. We improve on this severe limitation in the subsequent subsections.

+n⁡(1+1r)2∫𝒵𝔼z[∑i,j[Jz]i,j(zn,t,i−z^n,i)(zn,t,j−z^n,j)\displaystyle\quad+\frac{n(1+\frac{1}{r})}{2}\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{z}\bigg[\sum_{i,j}[J_{z}]_{i,j}(z_{n,t,i}-\hat{z}_{n,i})(z_{n,t,j}-\hat{z}_{n,j})
+o(∥zn,t−z∥2)μ(dz)]\displaystyle\quad+o\big({\|z_{n,t}-z\|^{2}}\big)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z)\bigg] (48)
≤1+r2​∫𝒵d​μ​(𝑑z)+o⁡(1)+1+1r2​∑i≥j|[Jz]i,j|​t2\displaystyle\leq\frac{1+r}{2}\int_{\mathcal{Z}}d\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z)+o(1)+\frac{1+\frac{1}{r}}{2}\sum_{i\geq j}|[J_{z}]_{i,j}|t^{2}
+∫𝒵𝔼z[o(n∥zn,t−z∥2)]μ(dz)\displaystyle\quad+\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\mathbb{E}_{z}\left[o\big(n{\|z_{n,t}-z\|^{2}}\big)\right]\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (49)
=(1+r)​d2+1+1r2​∑i≥j|[Jz]i,j|​t2+o⁡(1).\displaystyle=\frac{(1+r)d}{2}+\frac{1+\frac{1}{r}}{2}\sum_{i\geq j}|[J_{z}]_{i,j}|t^{2}+o(1). (50)

We now justify some of the steps above. In (44), the expectation is over the random zn,t​(z^ML​(Xn))z_{n,t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})) where Xn∼PX|Z=znX^{n}\sim P_{X|Z=z}^{n}; in (45) we used Jensen’s inequality and the convexity of the relative entropy; in (46) we used the Euclidean approximation of the relative entropy in (14) (Assumption (ii)); in (47) we used the inequality in (43); in (48) we used (15) (Assumption (iii)); and in (49) and (50) we used the definition of the lattice 𝒵n,t\mathcal{Z}_{n,t} resulting in the bound |zn,t,i−z^n,i|≤tn|z_{n,t,i}-\hat{z}_{n,i}|\leq\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} for all ii and nn.

Now since n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} is arbitrary,

lim¯n→∞⁡εb(2)​(fb,n,φn)≤1+r2​d+1+1r2​∑i≥j|[Jz]i,j|​t2\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})\leq\frac{1+r}{2}d+\frac{1+\frac{1}{r}}{2}\sum_{i\geq j}|[J_{z}]_{i,j}|t^{2} (51)

Since t>0t>0 is arbitrary, we may take t→0t\to 0 so the second term vanishes. Next, since r>0r>0 is arbitrary, we may take r→0r\to 0 so the first term converges to the asymptotic error bound of d2\frac{d}{2}. This proves the upper bound in (41).

We now consider visible case, which is simpler. In this case, we can replace the MLE z^n\hat{z}_{n} by zz, since the encoder has direct access to the parameter zz. Hence, the first terms in (47)–(51) are equal 00 and we obtain (40) as desired.∎

V-B Direct Part For Exponential Families

In the blind setting, the MDL encoder discussed in Section V-A has a non-vanishing error even in the asymptotic limit. To overcome this problem, we devise a novel method attaining zero error in the asymptotic limit. Since the method is more complicated in the general setting, and requires more assumptions (see Section V-C), we first assume that the distribution family forms an exponential family, and prove the direct part under the relative entropy criterion.

Lemma 2.

When {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} is an exponential family and Assumption (i) holds, we have

Rb(2)​(0)≤d2.\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(0)\leq\frac{d}{2}. (52)

Note that this indeed implies the direct part of (22) since Rb(2)​(δ2′)≤d2R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2}^{\prime})\leq\frac{d}{2} for all δ2′∈[0,∞)\delta_{2}^{\prime}\in[0,\infty). This significantly improves over the case where we do not assume that {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} is an exponential family in (41) of Lemma 1 since we could only prove that Rb(2)​(δ2′)≤d2R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2}^{\prime})\leq\frac{d}{2} for all δ2′∈[d2,∞)\delta_{2}^{\prime}\in[\frac{d}{2},\infty), which is much weaker. In other words, the blind code presented below for exponential families can realize the same error performance (which is asymptotically zero) as the visible code presented at the end of the proof of Lemma 1. We also observe that Assumption (i) holds for the kk-nomial example discussed in Section IV-D as the moment parameters 𝔼z​[Ti]\mathbb{E}_{z}[T_{i}] belong to [−1,1][-1,1], which is bounded.

Proof of Lemma 2.

First, to describe the encoder, we extract the sufficient statistics from the data, i.e., we calculate

η^i:=Yi(n)​(xn)n=1n∑j=1nYi(xj),∀i=1,…,d.\hat{\eta}_{i}:=\frac{Y_{i}^{(n)}(x^{n})}{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}Y_{i}(x_{j}),\quad\forall\,i=1,\ldots,d. (53)

Next we fix a lattice span t>0t>0 and consider the subset of quantized moment parameters ℋn,t:=tn​ℤd∩ℋ⊂ℋ\mathcal{H}_{n,t}:=\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{Z}^{d}\cap\mathcal{H}\subset\mathcal{H} where recall that ℋ={η⁡(z):z∈𝒵}\mathcal{H}=\{\eta(z):z\in\mathcal{Z}\} is the set of feasible moment parameters (cf. Section IV-C). Given the observed value of η^=(η^1,…,η^n)\hat{\eta}=(\hat{\eta}_{1},\ldots,\hat{\eta}_{n}), we choose the closest point in the lattice to it, i.e., we choose

βt​(η):=arg​minη′∈ℋn,t⁡‖η′−η‖.\beta_{t}(\eta):=\argmin_{\eta^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}_{n,t}}\|\eta^{\prime}-\eta\|. (54)

The encoder fb,nf_{\mathrm{b},n} is the map xn↦βt​(η^)x^{n}\mapsto\beta_{t}(\hat{\eta}). For this encoder, the memory size is |ℋn,t||\mathcal{H}_{n,t}|. Thus the coding length is log⁡|ℋn,t|=d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\log|\mathcal{H}_{n,t}|=\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1), where the dependence in tt is in the O⁡(1)O(1) term.

Now, we describe the decoder. Let Y(n)=(Y1(n),…,Yd(n))Y^{(n)}=(Y^{(n)}_{1},\ldots,Y^{(n)}_{d}) and η=(η1,…,ηd)\eta=(\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{d}). The decoder φn\varphi_{n} is the map

η¯↦1|βt−1​(η¯)|​∑η∈βt−1​(η¯)PXn|Y(n)=n​η.\bar{\eta}\mapsto\frac{1}{|\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{\eta})|}\sum_{\eta\in\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{\eta})}P_{X^{n}|Y^{(n)}=n\eta}. (55)

In other words, given the estimate βt​(η)∈ℋn,t\beta_{t}(\eta)\in\mathcal{H}_{n,t}, we consider a uniform mixture of all the distributions PXn|Y(n)=n​ηP_{X^{n}|Y^{(n)}=n\eta} where η\eta runs over all points in the lattice that map to βt​(η)\beta_{t}(\eta) under the encoding map in (54).

In the following calculation of the error, we first consider the scalar case in which d=1d=1 for simplicity. At the end of the proof, we show how to extend the ideas to the case where d>1d>1. A few additional notational conventions are needed. For each element η¯\bar{\eta}, denote the uniform distribution on the subset βt−1​(η¯)\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{\eta}) as Uβt−1​(η¯)U_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{\eta})}. Next, denote the transition kernel (channel) that maps the mean parameter η¯\bar{\eta} to the uniform distribution on the set βt−1​(η¯)\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{\eta}) (i.e., Uβt−1​(η¯)U_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{\eta})}) as Uβt−1​(Y)|YU_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(Y)|Y}. Denote the distribution of the random variable Y1(n)​(Xn)Y_{1}^{(n)}(X^{n}) when Xn∼PX|Z=znX^{n}\sim P_{X|Z=z}^{n} as PY1(n)|Z=zP_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z}. Let the variance of Y1(n)Y_{1}^{(n)} under distribution PX|Z=zP_{X|Z=z} be VzV_{z}. The normalizing linear transformation y↦n​(y−𝔼z​[Y1(n)])/Vzy\mapsto\sqrt{n}(y-\mathbb{E}_{z}[Y_{1}^{(n)}])/\sqrt{V_{z}} is denoted as gzg_{z}.

Since Y1(n)Y_{1}^{(n)} is a sufficient statistic relative to the exponential family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}, we know that for any error criterion (in particular the relative entropy criterion),

D(φn⋅fb,n⋅PX|Z=zn∥PX|Z=zn)\displaystyle D(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{b},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\,\|\,P_{X|Z=z}^{n})
=D(Uβt−1​(Y)|Y⋅PY1(n)|Z=z∥PY1(n)|Z=z)\displaystyle=D(U_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(Y)|Y}\cdot P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z}\,\|\,P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z}) (56)
=D((Uβt−1​(Y)|Y⋅PY1(n)|Z=z)⋅gz−1∥PY1(n)|Z=z⋅gz−1),\displaystyle=D\big((U_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(Y)|Y}\cdot P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z})\cdot g_{z}^{-1}\,\|\,P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z}\cdot g_{z}^{-1}\big), (57)

where the last equality follows from the fact that the function gzg_{z} is one-to-one. By the central limit theorem, PY1(n)|Z=z⋅gz−1P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z}\cdot g_{z}^{-1} converges to the standard normal distribution ϕ(u)∝exp(−u2/2)\phi(u)\propto\exp(-u^{2}/2). On the other hand, by the definition of Uβt−1​(Y)|YU_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(Y)|Y} (which results from the construction of the encoder in (54)), the distribution (Uβt−1​(Y)|Y⋅PY1(n)|Z=z)⋅gz−1(U_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(Y)|Y}\cdot P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z})\cdot g_{z}^{-1} converges to a quantization of the standard normal distribution with span tt, namely,

ϕt,α(u)∝ϕ(α+(j+1/2)t),∀u∈(α+jt,α+(j+1)t],\phi_{t,\alpha}(u)\propto\phi\big(\alpha+(j+1/2)t\big),\;\forall\,u\in(\alpha+jt,\alpha+(j+1)t], (58)

where α∈[0,t]\alpha\in[0,t] and the constant of proportionality in (58) is chosen so that ∫ℝϕt,α​(u)​𝑑u=1\int_{\mathbb{R}}\phi_{t,\alpha}(u)\,\mathrm{d}u=1. See Fig. 1 for an illustration of the probability density function in (58). Thus, we have the upper bound

lim¯n→∞D((Uβt−1​(Y)|Y⋅PY1(n)|Z=z)⋅gz−1∥PY1(n)|Z=z⋅gz−1)\displaystyle\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}D\big((U_{\beta_{t}^{-1}(Y)|Y}\cdot P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z})\cdot g_{z}^{-1}\,\|\,P_{Y_{1}^{(n)}|Z=z}\cdot g_{z}^{-1}\big)
≤supα∈[0,t]D(ϕt,α∥ϕ).\displaystyle\qquad\leq\sup_{\alpha\in[0,t]}D(\phi_{t,\alpha}\,\|\,\phi). (59)

Since the convergence in (59) is uniform on compact sets (compact convergence), we have

lim¯n→∞⁡εb(2)​(fb,n,φn)\displaystyle\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})
=lim¯n→∞∫𝒵D(φn⋅fb,n⋅PX|Z=zn∥PX|Z=zn)μ(dz)\displaystyle=\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\int_{\mathcal{Z}}D(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{b},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\,\|\,P_{X|Z=z}^{n})\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (60)
≤∫𝒵lim¯n→∞D(φn⋅fb,n⋅PX|Z=zn∥PX|Z=zn)μ(dz)\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}D(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{b},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\,\|\,P_{X|Z=z}^{n})\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (61)
≤supα∈[0,t]D(ϕt,α∥ϕ).\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\alpha\in[0,t]}D(\phi_{t,\alpha}\,\|\,\phi). (62)

Now since the above holds for all t>0t>0, we can let tt tend to 00 (so the size of the quantization regions decreases to 00). Consequently, the right-hand-side of (62) also tends to 00 and hence, limn→∞εb(2)​(fb,n,φn)=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})=0.

For general dimension d>1d>1, we can show the desired statement as follows. Let ϕ(d)\phi^{(d)} be the dd-dimensional standard normal distribution. Given α∈[0,t]d\alpha\in[0,t]^{d}, let ϕt,α(d)\phi^{(d)}_{t,\alpha} be the corresponding quantization of the dd-dimensional standard normal distribution with cutting point α\alpha and span tt (cf. (58) for the one-dimensional distribution). Then in the same way,

lim¯n→∞εb(2)(fb,n,φn)≤supα∈[0,t]dD(ϕt,α(d)∥ϕ(d)).\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})\leq\sup_{\alpha\in[0,t]^{d}}D(\phi_{t,\alpha}^{(d)}\,\|\,\phi^{(d)}). (63)

Similarly, we can take tt to tend to zero and the error criterion vanishes as n→∞n\to\infty. The logarithm of the memory size (coding length) is thus d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1). This proves Lemma 2. ∎

V-C Direct Part For The General Case

In this section we treat the general case (not necessarily exponential family). We prove the following lemma which establishes the direct part (upper bound) in the blind setting under the variational distance criterion as in (20).

Lemma 3.

Assuming (i), (ii), (iv), and (v), we have

Rb(1)​(0)≤d2.\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(0)\leq\frac{d}{2}. (64)

Note that this implies the upper bound to (20) because (64) implies that Rb(1)​(δ1′)≤d2R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(\delta_{1}^{\prime})\leq\frac{d}{2} for all δ1′∈[0,2)\delta_{1}^{\prime}\in[0,2).

Proof of Lemma 3.

Fix a lattice span t>0t>0 and choose the memory 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}_{n} to be the quantized parameter space (lattice) 𝒵n,t:=tn​ℤd∩𝒵⊂𝒵\mathcal{Z}_{n,t}:=\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{Z}^{d}\cap\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathcal{Z}. Given the observed MLE z^ML​(Xn)=z\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})=z, we choose the encoder output to be the closest point in this lattice, i.e.,

βt​(z):=arg​minz′∈𝒵n,t⁡‖z′−z‖.\displaystyle\beta_{t}(z):=\argmin_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}_{n,t}}\|z^{\prime}-z\|. (65)

The encoder fb,nf_{\mathrm{b},n} is the map from xn↦βt​(z^ML​(xn))x^{n}\mapsto\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(x^{n})). Thus the code has memory 𝒴n=𝒵n,t\mathcal{Y}_{n}=\mathcal{Z}_{n,t} in which the coding length is log⁡|𝒴n|=log|𝒵n,t|=d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\log|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|=\log|\mathcal{Z}_{n,t}|=\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1).

Now, to describe the decoder and the subsequent analysis, we use some simplified notation. Let YY and Y′Y^{\prime} denote the random variables βt​(z^ML​(Xn))\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})) and z^ML​(Xn)\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}) respectively. These can be thought of as the quantized MLE and the MLE respectively. As usual Z∈𝒵Z\in\mathcal{Z} is the original parameter. The decoder φn\varphi_{n} is then the following map from elements in the memory to distributions in 𝒫⁡(𝒳n)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}^{n}):

z¯↦1|βt−1​(z¯)|∑z∈βt−1​(z¯)PXn|Y′=z,Y=z¯.\bar{z}\mapsto\frac{1}{|\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{z})|}\sum_{z\in\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{z})}P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime}=z,Y=\bar{z}}. (66)

Essentially, the decoder takes the quantized MLE βt​(z^ML​(Xn))\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})) and outputs a uniform mixture over all “compatible” conditional distributions (i.e., all conditional distributions PXn|Y′=z,Y=z¯P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime}=z,Y=\bar{z}} whose parameter zz lies in the quantization cell βt−1​(z¯)\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{z})).

We now estimate the error. We first consider the case d=1d=1 for simplicity. For each element z¯\bar{z}, denote the uniform distribution on the subset βt−1​(z¯)\beta_{t}^{-1}(\bar{z}) as UY′|Y=z¯U_{Y^{\prime}|Y=\bar{z}}. We denote the transition kernel corresponding to the map z¯↦UY′|Y=z¯\bar{z}\mapsto U_{Y^{\prime}|Y=\bar{z}} as PXn|Y′,YP_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Y}. Then the decoder φn\varphi_{n} can alternatively be written as the map z↦PXn|Y′,Y=z⋅UY′|Y=zz\mapsto P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Y=z}\cdot U_{Y^{\prime}|Y=z}. Now the error measured according to the variational distance can be written as

εb(1)​(fb,n,φn)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})
=∫𝒵‖φn⋅fb,n⋅PXn|Z=z−PXn|Z=z‖1​μ​(𝑑z)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\left\|\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{b},n}\cdot P_{X^{n}|Z=z}-P_{X^{n}|Z=z}\right\|_{1}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (67)
=∫𝒵∥(PXn|Y′,Y⋅UY′|Y)×PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))|Z=z\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\big\|(P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Y}\cdot U_{Y^{\prime}|Y})\times P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))|Z=z}
−PXn|Z=z∥1μ(dz)\displaystyle\qquad-P_{X^{n}|Z=z}\big\|_{1}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (68)

where (68) follows from the definitions of the encoder PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))|Z=zP_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))|Z=z} (given the parameter is Z=zZ=z) and decoder PXn|Y′,Y=z⋅UY′|Y=zP_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Y=z}\cdot U_{Y^{\prime}|Y=z}. For clarity, we write PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))|Z=zP_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))|Z=z} for the distribution of the quantized MLE βt​(z^ML​(Xn))\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})) given that the samples XnX^{n} are independently generated from the distribution parametrized by z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, i.e., PX|Z=znP_{X|Z=z}^{n}. Let the integrand in (68) for fixed zz be denoted as εb(1)​(fb,n,φn,z)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n};z). By the triangle inequality,

εb(1)​(fb,n,φn,z)≤An+Bn,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n};z)\leq A_{n}+B_{n}, (69)

where the sequences AnA_{n} and BnB_{n} are defined as

An\displaystyle A_{n} :=∥(PXn|Y′,Y⋅UY′|Y)×PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))|Z=z\displaystyle:=\big\|(P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Y}\cdot U_{Y^{\prime}|Y})\times P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))|Z=z}
−PXn|Y′,Y⋅PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn)),Y′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=z∥1,\displaystyle\qquad-P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Y}\cdot P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})),Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z}\big\|_{1}, (70)

and

Bn\displaystyle B_{n} :=∥PXn|Y′,Y⋅PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn)),Y′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=z\displaystyle:=\big\|P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Y}\cdot P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})),Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z}
−PXn|Z=z∥1.\displaystyle\qquad-P_{X^{n}|Z=z}\big\|_{1}. (71)

Note that PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn)),Y′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=zP_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})),Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z} is the joint distribution of the quantized MLE βt​(z^ML​(Xn))\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})) and the true MLE z^ML​(Xn)\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}) given that the samples XnX^{n} are independently generated from the distribution parametrized by z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}. Now, by the data processing inequality for the variational distance (i.e., ‖PX|Y⋅PY|Z=z−PX|Y⋅QY|Z=z‖1≤‖PY|Z=z−QY|Z=z‖1\|P_{X|Y}\cdot P_{Y|Z=z}-P_{X|Y}\cdot Q_{Y|Z=z}\|_{1}\leq\|P_{Y|Z=z}-Q_{Y|Z=z}\|_{1}), the term AnA_{n} in (70) can be bounded as

An\displaystyle A_{n} ≤|UY′|Y×PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))|Z=z\displaystyle\leq\big\|U_{Y^{\prime}|Y}\times P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))|Z=z}
−PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn)),Y′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=z∥1\displaystyle\quad-P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})),Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z}\big\|_{1} (72)

We now analyze the right-hand-sides of (72) and (71) in turn.

By a similar reasoning as in the proof of Lemma 2, UY′|Y×PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))|Z=zU_{Y^{\prime}|Y}\times P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))|Z=z} converges to the quantization of the standard normal distribution ϕt,α\phi_{t,\alpha} (defined in (58)) by the local asymptotic normality assumption as stated in (16) (Assumption (iv)). Furthermore, since YY is a deterministic function of Y′Y^{\prime}, we have the relation PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn)),Y′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=z(y,y′)=PY′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=z(y)𝟙{y=βt(y′)}P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})),Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z}(y,y^{\prime})=P_{Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z}(y)\mathbbm{1}\{y=\beta_{t}(y^{\prime})\}. Hence, the distribution PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn)),Y′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=zP_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})),Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z} converges to the standard normal distribution ϕ\phi again by the local asymptotic normality assumption as stated in (16) (Assumption (iv)). Applying the triangle inequality to the right-hand-side of (72), we have

lim¯n→∞⁡An\displaystyle\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}A_{n}
≤lim¯n→∞{∥UY′|Y×PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))|Z=z−ϕt,α∥1\displaystyle\leq\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\Big\{\big\|U_{Y^{\prime}|Y}\times P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))|Z=z}-\phi_{t,\alpha}\big\|_{1}
+‖ϕt,α−ϕ‖1\displaystyle\qquad+\big\|\phi_{t,\alpha}-\phi\big\|_{1}
+∥ϕ−PY=βt​(z^ML​(Xn)),Y′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=z∥1}\displaystyle\qquad+\big\|\phi-P_{Y=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})),Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z}\big\|_{1}\Big\} (73)
≤supα∈[0,t]‖ϕt,α−ϕ‖1.\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\alpha\in[0,t]}\big\|\phi_{t,\alpha}-\phi\big\|_{1}. (74)

Now we analyze the right-hand-side of (71). First, note that Y′−z=z^ML​(Xn)−zY^{\prime}-z=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})-z behaves as Θ⁡(1n)\Theta(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}) with probability tending to one by the central limit theorem (local asymptotic normality). Since the quantization level is also of the order Θ⁡(1n)\Theta(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}), the difference Y−z=βt​(z^ML​(Xn))−zY-z=\beta_{t}(\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n}))-z also behaves as Θ⁡(1n)\Theta(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}) with probability tending to one. Hence, by regarding YY as the random variable 𝟙{Z=z~}\mathbbm{1}\{Z=\tilde{z}\} for some z~∈ℝd\tilde{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that differs from z∈𝒵⊂ℝdz\in\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} by Θ⁡(1n)\Theta(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}), we may write

Bn≤‖PXn|Y′,Z=z~⋅PY′=z^ML​(Xn)|Z=z−PXn|Z=z‖1.\displaystyle B_{n}\leq\big\|P_{X^{n}|Y^{\prime},Z=\tilde{z}}\cdot P_{Y^{\prime}=\hat{z}_{\mathrm{ML}}(X^{n})|Z=z}-P_{X^{n}|Z=z}\big\|_{1}. (75)

At this point, we may apply the local asymptotic sufficiency assumption as stated in (17) (Assumption (v)) to (75), yielding

limn→∞Bn=0.\lim_{n\to\infty}B_{n}=0. (76)

By (69), and similar compact convergence arguments as those leading from (60) to (62), we find that

lim¯n→∞⁡εb(1)​(fb,n,φn)≤supα∈[0,t]‖ϕt,α−ϕ‖1.\varlimsup_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})\leq\sup_{\alpha\in[0,t]}\big\|\phi_{t,\alpha}-\phi\big\|_{1}. (77)

Since this statement holds for all t>0t>0, taking the limit t→0t\to 0, we see that the asymptotic error limn→∞εb(1)​(fb,n,φn)=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{b}}^{(1)}(f_{\mathrm{b},n},\varphi_{n})=0. So in the general case for d=1d=1, we can achieve a memory length (log of memory size or coding length) of 12​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\frac{1}{2}\log n+O(1).

The case in which d>1d>1 can be analyzed in a completely analogous manner and we can conclude that a memory length of d2​log⁡n+O⁡(1)\frac{d}{2}\log n+O(1) can be achieved. ∎

VI Proofs of Converse Parts of Theorem 1

In this section, we prove the converse parts (lower bounds) to Theorem 1. We will only focus on the visible cases in (18) and (19) because according to (12), a converse for the visible case implies the same for the blind case. Essentially, by (7), a visible code cannot be outperformed by a blind code.

Since our problem is closely related to Clarke and Barron’s formula for the relative entropy between a parametrized distribution and a mixture distribution [24, 25], we clarify the relation between our problem and this formula. To clarify this relation, in Section VI-A, we prove a weak converse, namely, the impossibility of further compression from a rate of d2\frac{d}{2} when the variational distance error criterion is asymptotically zero. This can be shown by a simple combination of Clarke and Barron’s formula and the uniform continuity of mutual information [31] (also called Fannes inequality [32] in quantum information). Since the variational distance goes to zero when the relative entropy goes to zero, the weak converse under the variational distance criterion implies the weak converse under the relative entropy criterion. Hence, the arguments in Section VI-A demonstrate the weak converse under both error criteria. These arguments clarify the relation between Clarke and Barron’s formula and our problem. However, to the best of our knowledge, the strong converse parts cannot be shown via Clarke and Barron’s formula, i.e., they require novel methods. Furthermore, there is no similar relation between the strong converse parts under the variational distance and the relative entropy. This is because there is no relation between code rates when the relative entropy is arbitrarily large and when the variational distance is arbitrarily close to 22, i.e., its maximum value. So, we need to prove two types of strong converse parts for each of the two error criteria. In Section VI-B, we prove a strong converse for the relative entropy error criterion using the Pythagorean theorem for the relative entropy, thus demonstrating (19). In Section VI-C, we prove a strong converse for the variational distance error criterion by a different, and novel, method, thus demonstrating (18).

VI-A Weak Converse Under Both Criteria Based On Clarke And Barron’s Formula

In this section, we prove the following weak converse.

Lemma 4.

The following lower bound holds

Rv(1)​(0)≥d2.R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(1)}(0)\geq\frac{d}{2}. (78)

This is, in fact, only a weak converse since asymptotically the error measured according to the variational distance must tend to zero. It is insufficient to show (18) but we present the proof to demonstrate the connection between Clarke and Barron’s result in (79) to follow and the problem we study. Here, we are only concerned with the variational distance criterion because a weak converse for this criterion implies the same for the relative entropy criterion.

Proof of Lemma 4.

We first assume that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a finite set. At the end, we show how to relax this condition. We recall that Clarke and Barron [24, 25] showed for a parametric family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} that

∫𝒵D(PX|Z=zn∥∫𝒵PX|Z=z′nν(dz′))μ(dz)\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{Z}}D\bigg(P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\,\Big\|\,\int_{\mathcal{Z}}P_{X|Z=z^{\prime}}^{n}\,\nu(\mathrm{d}z^{\prime})\bigg)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z)
=d2logn2​π​e+D(μ∥ν)−D(μ∥μJ)+logCJ+o(1),\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2}\log\frac{n}{2\pi\mathrm{e}}+D(\mu\|\nu)-D(\mu\|\mu_{\mathrm{J}})+\log C_{\mathrm{J}}+o(1), (79)

where JzJ_{z} is the Fisher information matrix defined in (13), μJ​(d​z):=1CJ​det​Jz​d​z\mu_{\mathrm{J}}(\mathrm{d}z):=\frac{1}{C_{\mathrm{J}}}\mathrm{det}\sqrt{J_{z}}\,\mathrm{d}z is the so-called Jeffrey’s prior [25] and CJ:=∫𝒵det​Jz​𝑑zC_{\mathrm{J}}:=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\mathrm{det}\sqrt{J_{z}}\,\mathrm{d}z is the normalization factor. When ν=μ\nu=\mu, the left-hand-side of (79) is precisely the mutual information I⁡(Xn,Z)I(X^{n};Z) where the pair of random variables (Xn,Z)(X^{n},Z) is distributed according to PXn,Z​(xn,z):=PX|Z=zn​(xn)​μ​(z)P_{X^{n},Z}(x^{n},z):=P_{X|Z=z}^{n}(x^{n})\mu(z). See [33] for an overview of approximations similar to (79) in the context of universal source coding and model selection.

For the purpose of proving the weak converse, we assume that we are given a sequence of codes {𝒞v,n:=(fv,n,φn)}n∈ℕ\{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}:=(f_{\mathrm{v},n},\varphi_{n})\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}} satisfying the condition that the error measured according to the variational distance vanishes, i.e.,

δn:=εv(1)​(𝒞v,n)→0,as ​n→∞.\delta_{n}:=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^{(1)}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n})\to 0,\quad\mbox{as }n\to\infty. (80)

Now let the code distribution be P𝒞v,n​(xn,z):=(φn⋅fv,n​(z))​(xn)​μ​(z)P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}(x^{n},z):=(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z))(x^{n})\mu(z) where φn⋅fv,n​(z)\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z) is defined in (5) and (φn⋅fv,n​(z))​(xn)(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z))(x^{n}) is the evaluation of φn⋅fv,n​(z)\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z) at xnx^{n}. Then, the definition of the error in the visible case in (6) and (80) implies that the variational distance between the code distribution and the generating distribution satisfies

‖P𝒞v,n−PXn,Z‖1≤δn,\left\|P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}-P_{X^{n},Z}\right\|_{1}\leq\delta_{n}, (81)

for some sequence δn=o⁡(1)\delta_{n}=o(1). Since |𝒳||\mathcal{X}| is finite, we can use the method of types to find a set of sufficient statistics for the data (cf. Section IV-D). Indeed, we can form a set of sufficient statistics relative to the family {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}. Let us call the sufficient statistics Gn:𝒳n→ℝ|𝒳|G_{n}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}|}. The output cardinality of GnG_{n} is |Gn​(𝒳n)|=|{Gn​(xn):xn∈𝒳n}|≤(n+1)|𝒳|−1|G_{n}(\mathcal{X}^{n})|=|\{G_{n}(x^{n}):x^{n}\in\mathcal{X}^{n}\}|\leq(n+1)^{|\mathcal{X}|-1} because we can take the type of xnx^{n} to be the sufficient statistic, i.e., Gn​(xn)=type⁡(xn)G_{n}(x^{n})=\mathrm{type}(x^{n}). By the data processing inequality for the variational distance, we have

‖P𝒞v,n⋅Gn−1−PXn,Z⋅Gn−1‖1≤δn.\left\|P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}-P_{X^{n},Z}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}\right\|_{1}\leq\delta_{n}. (82)

In the following we use a subscript to denote the distribution of the random variables in the arguments of the mutual information functional, so for example IPA​B(A;B)=∑aPA(a)D(PB|A(⋅|a)∥PB)I_{P_{AB}}(A;B)=\sum_{a}P_{A}(a)D(P_{B|A}(\cdot|a)\|P_{B}). Now, we notice that

IPXn,Z⋅Gn−1​(Gn​(Xn),Z)\displaystyle I_{P_{X^{n},Z}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}}(G_{n}(X^{n});Z) =IPXn,Z​(Xn,Z),and\displaystyle=I_{P_{X^{n},Z}}(X^{n};Z),\quad\mbox{and} (83)
IP𝒞v,n⋅Gn−1​(Gn​(Xn),Z)\displaystyle I_{P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}}(G_{n}(X^{n});Z) ≤IP𝒞v,n​(Xn,Z)\displaystyle\leq I_{P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}}(X^{n};Z) (84)

where (83) follows from the definition of sufficient statistics and (84) follows from the data processing inequality for mutual information. In addition, by the uniform continuity of mutual information [31, 32] and (82), we have

|IPXn,Z⋅Gn−1​(Gn​(Xn),Z)−IP𝒞v,n⋅Gn−1​(Gn​(Xn),Z)|\displaystyle\big|I_{P_{X^{n},Z}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}}(G_{n}(X^{n});Z)-I_{P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}}(G_{n}(X^{n});Z)\big|
≤δn​log⁡((n+1)|𝒳|−1)+ξ⁡(δn),\displaystyle\quad\leq\delta_{n}\log((n+1)^{|\mathcal{X}|-1})+\xi(\delta_{n}), (85)

where ξ⁡(x):=−x​log⁡x\xi(x):=-x\log x. We define the upper bound between the two mutual information quantities in (85) as δn′:=δn​log⁡((n+1)|𝒳|−1)+ξ⁡(δn)\delta_{n}^{\prime}:=\delta_{n}\log((n+1)^{|\mathcal{X}|-1})+\xi(\delta_{n}) and note that δn′=o⁡(log⁡n)\delta_{n}^{\prime}=o(\log n).

Define the joint distribution of the encoder and the parameter as Pfv,n​(y,z):=Pfv,n​(z)​(y)​μ​(z)P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}}(y,z):=P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)\mu(z) (recall the code is visible so fv,nf_{\mathrm{v},n} has access to zz). Consider the mutual information between the parameter ZZ and the memory index YY,

log⁡|𝒴n|\displaystyle\log|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|
≥IPfv,n​(Y,Z)\displaystyle\geq I_{P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}}}(Y;Z) (86)
=∫𝒵D(fv,n(z)∥∫𝒵fv,n(z′)μ(dz′))μ(dz)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}D\left(f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)\,\Big\|\,\int_{\mathcal{Z}}f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z^{\prime})\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z^{\prime})\right)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (87)
≥∫𝒵D(φn⋅fv,n(z)∥∫𝒵φn⋅fv,n(z′)μ(dz′))μ(dz)\displaystyle\geq\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\!D\left(\!\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)\Big\|\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z^{\prime})\mu(\mathrm{d}z^{\prime})\right)\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (88)
=IP𝒞v,n​(Xn,Z)\displaystyle=I_{P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}}(X^{n};Z) (89)
≥IP𝒞v,n⋅Gn−1​(Gn​(Xn),Z)\displaystyle\geq I_{P_{\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}}(G_{n}(X^{n});Z) (90)
≥IPXn,Z⋅Gn−1​(Gn​(Xn),Z)−δn′\displaystyle\geq I_{P_{X^{n},Z}\cdot G_{n}^{-1}}(G_{n}(X^{n});Z)-\delta_{n}^{\prime} (91)
=IPXn,Z​(Xn,Z)−δn′\displaystyle=I_{P_{X^{n},Z}}(X^{n};Z)-\delta_{n}^{\prime} (92)
=∫𝒵D(PX|Z=zn∥∫𝒵PX|Z=z′nμ(dz′))μ(dz)−δn′\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}D\left(P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\,\Big\|\,\int_{\mathcal{Z}}P_{X|Z=z^{\prime}}^{n}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z^{\prime})\right)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z)-\delta_{n}^{\prime} (93)
=d2logn2​π​e−D(μ∥μJ)+logCJ+o(1)−δn′\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2}\log\frac{n}{2\pi\mathrm{e}}-D(\mu\|\mu_{\mathrm{J}})+\log C_{\mathrm{J}}+o(1)-\delta_{n}^{\prime} (94)
=d2​log⁡n+o⁡(log⁡n).\displaystyle=\frac{d}{2}\log n+o(\log n). (95)

In the above chain, (87), (89), and (93) follow from the definition of mutual information, (88) follows from the data processing inequality for the relative entropy, (90) follows from the data processing inequality for mutual information, (91) follows from the uniform continuity of mutual information as stated in (85), (92) follows from the notion of sufficient statistics as seen in (83), and (94) follows from Clarke and Barron’s formula [24] with ν=μ\nu=\mu in (79). We conclude that if a sequence of codes is such that the variational distance vanishes as in (80), the memory size |𝒴n|≥nd2+o⁡(1)|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|\geq n^{\frac{d}{2}+o(1)}.

Now, when 𝒳\mathcal{X} is not a finite set, we can choose a finite disjoint partition {𝒮w}w∈𝒲\{\mathcal{S}_{w}\}_{w\in\mathcal{W}} of 𝒳\mathcal{X} satisfying the following conditions: (i) |𝒲||\mathcal{W}| is finite and (ii) ∪w∈𝒲𝒮w=𝒳\cup_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\mathcal{S}_{w}=\mathcal{X}. Now, we define the parametric family PW|Z=z​(w):=PX|Z=z​(𝒮w)P_{W|Z=z}(w):=P_{X|Z=z}(\mathcal{S}_{w}). Clearly, we can go through the above proof with the finite-support random variable WW in place of XX. Now, when the code reconstructs the original family {PX|Z=zn}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}, clearly it also reconstructs the quantized family {PX|W=wn}w∈𝒲\{P_{X|W=w}^{n}\}_{w\in\mathcal{W}}. In essence, reconstructing the latter is “easier” than the former. Since (78) holds for the family {PX|W=wn}w∈𝒲\{P_{X|W=w}^{n}\}_{w\in\mathcal{W}} it must also hold for {PX|Z=zn}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}. This completes the proof of (78). ∎

VI-B Strong Converse Under The Relative Entropy Criterion

In this section, we prove the following strong converse result using the Pythagorean theorem for the relative entropy.

Lemma 5.

The following lower bound holds

Rv(2)​(δ2)≥d2,∀δ2∈[0,∞).R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2})\geq\frac{d}{2},\quad\forall\,\delta_{2}\in[0,\infty). (96)

This proves the lower bound to (19). The proof hinges on the Pythagorean formula for the relative entropy and a geometric argument also contained in Rissanen’s work [22].

Proof of Lemma 5.

Given probability measures {Pi}i∈ℐ\{P_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} and QQ, and a probability mass function {pi}i∈ℐ\{p_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}, the Pythagorean formula for relative entropy [26] states that

∑i∈ℐpiD(Pi∥Q)=D(∑i∈ℐpiPi∥Q)+∑i∈ℐpiD(Pi∥∑j∈ℐpjPj).\!\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}p_{i}D(P_{i}\|Q)\!=\!D\bigg(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}p_{i}P_{i}\Big\|Q\bigg)\!+\!\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}p_{i}D\bigg(P_{i}\Big\|\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}p_{j}P_{j}\bigg). (97)

In the following, we show that if the memory size |𝒴n||\mathcal{Y}_{n}| is too small, say nd2​(1−ϵ)n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)} for some fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0, then the error εv(2)​(𝒞v,n)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^{(2)}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}) tends to infinity as nn grows.

Consider any code 𝒞v,n=(fv,n,φn)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}=(f_{\mathrm{v},n},\varphi_{n}) with memory size |𝒴n|=nd2​(1−ϵ)|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|=n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)}. Let Pfv,n​(z)(y)=Pr{fv,n(z)=y}P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)=\Pr\{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)=y\} be the probability that the index in the memory Y∈𝒴nY\in\mathcal{Y}_{n} takes on the value yy when the parameter is z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} under the random encoder mapping fv,nf_{\mathrm{v},n}. Then an application of the Pythagorean theorem in (97) yields

D(∑y∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y)φn(y)∥PX|Z=zn)\displaystyle D\bigg(\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)\varphi_{n}(y)\bigg\|P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\bigg)
=∑y∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y)D(φn(y)∥PX|Z=zn)\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)D(\varphi_{n}(y)\|P_{X|Z=z}^{n})
−∑y∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y)D(φn(y)∥∑y′∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y′)φn(y′)).\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}\!\!P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)D\bigg(\!\varphi_{n}(y)\bigg\|\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}\!\!P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y^{\prime})\varphi_{n}(y^{\prime})\bigg). (98)

Hence, by integrating (98) over all z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, we obtain

εv(2)​(fv,n,φn)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^{(2)}(f_{\mathrm{v},n},\varphi_{n})
=∫𝒵D(φn⋅fv,n(z)∥PX|Z=zn)μ(dz)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}D\big(\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)\big\|P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\big)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (99)
=∫𝒵D(∑y∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y)φn(y)∥PX|Z=zn)μ(dz)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}D\bigg(\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)\varphi_{n}(y)\bigg\|P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\bigg)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z) (100)
=∫𝒵∑y∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y)[D(φn(y)∥PX|Z=zn)\displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)\Bigg[D\big(\varphi_{n}(y)\big\|P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\big)
−D(φn(y)∥∑y′∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y′)φn(y′))]μ(dz).\displaystyle\quad-D\bigg(\varphi_{n}(y)\bigg\|\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y^{\prime})\varphi_{n}(y^{\prime})\bigg)\Bigg]\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z). (101)

We analyze both terms in (101) in turn.

For the first term, we use an argument similar to that for the proof of Theorem 1(a) in Rissanen [22]. Note that since the size of |𝒴n||\mathcal{Y}_{n}| is nd2​(1−ϵ)n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)}, the set 𝒮n,ϵ\mathcal{S}_{n,\epsilon} of all possible distributions output by the decoder φn\varphi_{n} cannot exceed nd2​(1−ϵ)n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)}, i.e., |𝒮n,ϵ|=|{φn​(y):y∈𝒴n}|≤|𝒴n|=nd2​(1−ϵ)|\mathcal{S}_{n,\epsilon}|=|\{\varphi_{n}(y):y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}\}|\leq|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|=n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)}. For any given z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z}, let the closest distribution in 𝒮n,ϵ\mathcal{S}_{n,\epsilon} have parameter z′∈𝒵z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}. Since 𝒵∈ℝd\mathcal{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is bounded, we can estimate the (order of the) ℓ2\ell_{2} distance between zz and z′z^{\prime}, i.e., Δ:=‖z−z′‖\Delta:=\|z-z^{\prime}\|. If zz is a point in general position in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, then Δ\Delta is of the same order as rr, where rr is the largest radius of the nd2​(1−ϵ)n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)} disjoint spheres contained in 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Since the volume spheres of radius rr in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is proportional to rdr^{d}, we have that

Kd⋅rd⋅nd2​(1−ϵ)≥vol⁡(𝒵),K_{d}\cdot r^{d}\cdot n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)}\geq\mathrm{vol}(\mathcal{Z}), (102)

where KdK_{d} is a constant that depends only on the dimension dd. Since vol⁡(𝒵)\mathrm{vol}(\mathcal{Z}) does not depend on nn (it also only depends on dd) and Δ=Θ⁡(r)\Delta=\Theta(r),22 2 The implied constants in the Ω⁡(⋅)\Omega(\,\cdot\,) notations used in (103), (104), and (106) are all assumed to be positive.

Δ=Ω⁡(n−12​(1−ϵ)).\Delta=\Omega(n^{-\frac{1}{2}(1-\epsilon)}). (103)

At the same time, by the Euclidean approximation of relative entropy in (14), D(PX|Z=z′n∥PX|Z=zn)=Ω(n∥z−z′∥2)=Ω(nϵ)D(P_{X|Z=z^{\prime}}^{n}\|P_{X|Z=z}^{n})=\Omega(n\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2})=\Omega(n^{\epsilon}). Thus the first term in (101) scales as

∫𝒵∑y∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y)D(φn(y)∥PX|Z=zn)μ(dz)=Ω(nϵ).\!\!\!\!\!\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}\!\!P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)D\big(\varphi_{n}(y)\big\|P_{X|Z=z}^{n}\big)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}z)=\Omega(n^{\epsilon}). (104)

On the other hand the second term in (101) is a conditional mutual information. In particular, it can be upper bounded as

∫𝒵∑y∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y)D(φn(y)∥∑y′∈𝒴nPfv,n​(z)(y′)φn(y′))μ(dz)\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{Z}}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}\!P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y)D\bigg(\!\varphi_{n}(y)\bigg\|\!\sum_{y^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Y}_{n}}\!\!\!P_{f_{\mathrm{v},n}(z)}(y^{\prime})\varphi_{n}(y^{\prime})\bigg)\mu(\mathrm{d}z)
=I⁡(Xn;Y|Z)≤H⁡(Y)≤d2​(1−ϵ)​log⁡n.\displaystyle=I(X^{n};Y|Z)\leq H(Y)\leq\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)\log n. (105)

Note that the random variables in the information quantities above are computed with respect to the distribution induced by the visible code 𝒞v,n=(fv,n,φn)\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{v},n}=(f_{\mathrm{v},n},\varphi_{n}).

Combining (101), (104), and (105), we obtain

εv(2)​(fv,n,φn)≥Ω⁡(nϵ)−d2​(1−ϵ)​log⁡n→∞.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}}^{(2)}(f_{\mathrm{v},n},\varphi_{n})\geq\Omega(n^{\epsilon})-\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)\log n\to\infty. (106)

Hence, with a memory size of nd2​(1−ϵ)n^{\frac{d}{2}(1-\epsilon)}, the error computed according to the relative entropy criterion for any visible code diverges. This completes the proof of (96). ∎

VI-C Strong Converse Under The Variational Distance Criterion

In this section, we prove the following strong converse statement with respect to the variational distance error criterion.

Lemma 6.

The following lower bound holds

Rv(1)​(δ1)≥d2,∀δ1∈[0,2).R_{\mathrm{v}}^{(1)}(\delta_{1})\geq\frac{d}{2},\quad\forall\,\delta_{1}\in[0,2). (107)

Now, we can treat each dimension separately and apply the above argument to yield the same contradiction when the memory size is too small. ∎

VII Discussion and Future Research Directions

In this paper, we have considered the approximate reconstruction of a generating distribution PX|Z=znP_{X|Z=z}^{n} from a compressed version of a source XnX^{n} (the blind setting) or the parameter of generating distribution zz itself (the visible setting). We have shown using various notions of approximate sufficient statistics that when nn i.i.d. observations XnX^{n} are available, the length of the optimal code in most cases and under suitable regularity conditions is d2​log⁡n+o⁡(log⁡n)\frac{d}{2}\log n+o(\log n). In the process of deriving our results, we have strengthened the achievability part based on Rissanen’s MDL principle [21, 22]. We have also proved strong converses, thus strengthening the utility of Clarke and Barron’s formula [24, 25], which, by itself, only leads to a weak converse under the variational distance error criterion.

There are three promising avenues for future research:

  1. 1.

    It is natural to question whether the assumption of {PX|Z=z}z∈𝒵\{P_{X|Z=z}\}_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} being an exponential family is necessary to achieve Rb(2)​(δ2′)=d2,R_{\mathrm{b}}^{(2)}(\delta_{2}^{\prime})=\frac{d}{2}, for all δ2′∈[0,∞)\delta_{2}^{\prime}\in[0,\infty) in (22) (i.e., asymptotically zero error). We would like to remove this somewhat restrictive assumption if possible.

  2. 2.

    It is also natural to wonder about the scaling and form of the second-order term in the optimal code length log⁡|𝒴n|\log|\mathcal{Y}_{n}|. It is known from Theorem 1 that, in most cases, the first-order term scales as d2​log⁡n\frac{d}{2}\log n. Our achievability results based on Lemmas 1–3 suggest that the second-order term is of the constant order O⁡(1)O(1). Establishing that this is indeed a constant and the dependence of this constant as a function of δ≥0\delta\geq 0, the bound on the error, would be of significant theoretical and practical interest.

  3. 3.

    Since there are many distance “metrics” that may be used for measuring distances between two distributions (e.g., Csiszár’s ff-divergences) [34], it may also be fruitful to study the asymptotics of the optimal code length log⁡|𝒴n|\log|\mathcal{Y}_{n}| when other distance measures beyond the relative entropy and variational distance are used to quantify the discrepancy between PX|Z=znP_{X|Z=z}^{n} and φn⋅fv,n⋅PX|Z=zn\varphi_{n}\cdot f_{\mathrm{v},n}\cdot P_{X|Z=z}^{n} (in the blind setting).
